segments.text: The film is cold, not the cold of a refrigerated cabinet,
not the cold of a climate-controlled storage room,
the cold of something that has travelled up from a depth
where the temperature never changes,
where the water is one or two degrees above freezing,
and has been that temperature for millions of years
and will be that temperature long after any human concern for it
has ended. The metal housing is still dripping.
Harold Kovac sets it on the table in the ship's darkroom
and feels the chill of it through the cloth he uses to wipe his hands,
and then he sets the cloth aside, and then he begins.
The red safe light makes everything the same colour.
Hands, the tray, the chemical bath, developer first, then stop bath, then fixer.
The smell of acetic acid and silver compounds,
the specific sharp sour smell of photographic chemistry,
the smell that has permanently attached itself to every darkroom in the world,
has developed film in this room for 11 months.
His hands know the order of things without being told.
Retrieve the housing, extract the cartridge, load the developing tank in complete darkness,
the red light off, hands alone doing what hands alone must do in the total dark,
then the sequence, then the timer, then wait.
The ship moves under him. The USNS Eltonin is 11 months into its Antarctic research program,
currently on its 15th voyage, currently somewhere in the South Pacific,
currently a long way from anything. Through the walls of the darkroom,
the engine makes its continuous assertion against the water.
The red light is on again. The timer runs, then the film.
He pulls it from the tank in the red light and holds it up, frame by frame.
The strobe has fired throughout the deployment. Once every few seconds, automatically,
a camera toad on a cable far below the hull, illuminating the sea floor for a fraction of
a second each time. Most frames are what they are supposed to be. Gray sediment, the featureless
abyssal plain, the flat gray of 4,000 meters of accumulated silt, the ocean floor doing what
the ocean floor does in this region, which is nothing and nothing and nothing. Frame 1031,
gray sediment, expected. Frame 1033, gray sediment, expected. Frame 1032,
something standing in the sediment where nothing should stand.
He holds the frame up to the safe light, then he holds it closer. The safe light is red
and the film is negative and what he is looking at resolves slowly as his eyes adjust to what
being asked to read, a vertical form rising from the flat gray of the sea floor,
topped with horizontal projections. Not one, but several, arranged at right angles to the central
shaft, branching outward with a regularity that the eye catches before the mind has decided what
it is looking at. The thing is symmetrical. Whatever it is, its left side mirrors its right
side with a precision that soft sediment does not produce. The ocean floor does not make this shape.
The ocean floor makes softness and accumulation and the slow drift of things settling. Not this.
This looks placed. He stays with it for a long time. The film strip between his fingers,
the red light overhead, the ship moving beneath him, then he turns it around,
holds it from the other side, the same image reversed, still symmetrical.
Still standing upright in the sediment, still wrong in the way that a thing is wrong when it
belongs to a category that does not exist in the place where you have found it. He carries the frame
to the senior scientist on the night watch. The scientist takes it, holds it up to the light,
looks at it for a while, then he says it is probably biological. He says there are sponges
at these depths that form symmetrical structures. He says the deep ocean is full of things that
look designed because design and biology arrive at the same solutions through different processes.
He hands the frame back. Kovac writes in his notebook that night.
Frame 1032. I pulled it from the bath and held it up to the safe light,
and I did not understand what I was looking at. The sediment is flat.
There is nothing on the bottom in any of the other frames from this deployment.
Frame 1031 is mud. Frame 1033 is mud. Frame 1032 has something standing in the mud that
should not be standing in anything. He writes one more line. He did not sound convinced.
He sounded like a man who had an answer available, and was using it because the alternative was
having no answer. Kovac's notebook. A personal diary, not part of the ship's official record,
will spend the next 37 years in a box. His wife will donate his effects to a maritime
museum in San Diego in 2001. A volunteer will catalog the notebook three years after that,
noting its contents briefly, filing it. The entry for August 29th, 1964,
will sit in that catalog unread, while the question in frame 1032 continues to have no answer.
What is in frame 1032? That is where this investigation begins.
The photograph shows the following. A vertical shaft. A single central column,
rising from soft gray sediment. From this shaft, horizontal projections extend outward
at right angles. Not one projection. Several. Spaced with a regularity that is apparent even
in the image's imperfect black and white, the projections are symmetrical, the same number
on each side at the same angles. The whole structure stands approximately 60 centimetres tall.
It stands alone. The sediment around it is unbroken. Nothing else rises from the flat gray of the sea
floor. In any direction the image can show. The photograph is black and white. The image quality
is what deep sea photography in 1964 produced. Not fine. Not clear by any modern standard.
The strobe illumination uneven. The geometry of the lens distorting the edges.
The object at the centre of frame 1032 is not perfectly resolved. The available detail is limited.
And yet, the symmetry is unmistakable. Horizontal projections at 90 degree angles
from a central vertical shaft. The same arrangement, each side mirroring the other,
standing upright in the mud. It looks like an antenna.
That is not a metaphor. And it is not interpretation. It is a description of what the
photograph shows to anyone who looks at it. A vertical shaft. Horizontal crossbars at regular
intervals. The arrangement that human engineers arrived at, independently for the purpose of
transmitting and receiving electromagnetic signals across distance. That shape in the sediment
at the bottom of the South Pacific. Now the depth, the coordinates where the photograph was taken.
59 degrees. Seven minutes south. 105 degrees. Three minutes west.
In the South Pacific, approximately 1000 miles west of Cape Horn, in the South
Eastern Pacific basin. Not the South Atlantic. This detail matters because the fringe literature
over the decades has repeatedly placed the photograph in the wrong ocean.
The coordinates are documented. The ocean is the Pacific. The depth at those coordinates.
3,904 meters.
Righted out. 3,904 meters. 12,808 feet. Two and a half miles below the surface of the Pacific.
Below that surface. Darkness. Below approximately 1000 meters, no sunlight penetrates. The photograph
was taken in permanent darkness. A darkness that has never been interrupted by any light source
except the strobe of a toad camera for a fraction of a second on August 29th, 1964.
The pressure at that depth. 390 atmospheres. 390 times the pressure at the surface of the earth.
Every square inch of the camera housing was absorbing the weight of 3,900 meters of ocean.
The metal housing that Kovac retrieved from the cable, the housing that dripped cold onto his
table, had been sitting in conditions that would reduce a human body to nothing in less
than a second. The temperature at that depth. 1 to 2 degrees Celsius. Not freezing. Just above it.
Permanently. Not cold in the way that a winter morning is cold. Not cold in the way that cold
weather is cold. But cold in the way that a thing is cold when warmth has never reached it.
And never will. The sea floor at those coordinates is one of the most isolated places on the surface
of this planet. No sunlight. No warmth. No current strong enough to disturb the silt. The sediment
at that depth is fine grained clay and silt that has been accumulating for millions of years.
Falling slowly from above. Each layer settling on the last. Building a record of time that no one

right angles. The camera was automated. No one saw the object in real time. The film was in the
housing for hours before it reached Kovac's hands. The camera did not know what it photographed.
The strobe fired on its timer. The shutter opened. The shutter closed. The film advanced.
The camera was pulled back up. The housing was retrieved. The film was developed.
No one saw it until the dark room. August 1964. The U.S. N.S. L. Tannen. The Southern Ocean. South

The camera system that took the photograph is a toad unit. A housing on a cable dragged along

The strobe fires. The film advances. If something is there, the film records it.
If nothing is there, the film records the sediment. On August 29, 1964, during the 15th

The film advances. The strobe fires again. Frame 1032 receives whatever is standing

Frame 1033 receives gray sediment. The camera does not stop. The ship does not stop.
The deployment continues. And the camera continues. And the strobe continues to fire.
And the film continues to receive gray sediment. And then the deployment ends.
And the cable brings the housing back up. And it drips on Kovac's table. And he goes into the

The Eltonin has docked at Auckland, New Zealand, for overhaul. A scientist who has examined the
photograph, a Dr. Thomas Hopkins, speaks to a reporter. On December the 5th, 1964,
the New Zealand Herald publishes a story. The headline, Puzzle Picture from Seabed.
The story quotes Hopkins directly. The object, he says, is fairly symmetrical.
And the offshoots are all 90 degrees apart. He says the structure seems too extremely
symmetrical to correspond to a natural formation. Too extremely symmetrical. That phrase in print,
on December the 5th, 1964, is the moment the photograph enters the public record.
Hopkins is not claiming what it is. He is noting what it cannot be easily accounted for.
Too symmetrical. The observation is not theoretical. It is visual. Anyone can look at the photograph
and see the symmetry. Hopkins is saying what the image says. The question goes into the record.
It will not come out of the record for 60 years. And counting.
Seven years pass. In 1971, two geologists publish a book. The book is called The Face of the Deep.
The authors are Bruce Heeson, a geologist at the Lamont Doherty Geological Observatory of
Columbia University, and Charles Hollister, a marine geologist at the Woods Hole Oceanographic
Institution. The book is a catalogue of the deep sea floor. Photographs, descriptions, analysis.
The first systematic effort to describe what the ocean bottom actually looks like, region by region,
depth by depth, assembled from years of photographic surveys. The Eltonin antenna
photograph is in the book. Heeson and Hollister identify the object. They give it a name,
Claderheiser Concrescence, later reclassified as Chondrocladia Concrescence, a carnivorous
deep sea sponge of the family Claderheiserdei. The identification is accepted.
Here is what the science says. Chondrocladia Concrescence was first described in 1880
by the German marine biologist Otto Schmidt from specimens collected by dredging in the Gulf of
Mexico. It is a carnivorous sponge. Unlike most sponges, which filter particles from the water,
Claderheiserd sponges capture small crustaceans using microscopic hooks on their branches.
The species forms a central stalk with perpendicular branches. The branches arranged in a geometry
that the taxonomic description characterizes as regular. It lives at abyssal depths.
In the cold, permanent dark of the deep ocean floor. It is not common, but it is known.
It has been documented. It exists. The identification of the Eltonin object as
Chondrocladia Concrescence closes the case for marine biology. The case has been closed since 1971.
The object is a sponge. The perpendicular branches are the documented morphology of the species.
The symmetry is what deep sea carnivorous sponges of this family produce.
The photograph is of a biological organism at its natural depth,
doing what organisms of this type do. The case is closed. The investigation settles into this.
It is the right place to settle. The identification comes from two credentialed scientists.
Working from the photograph. Applying established taxonomic knowledge to an observed specimen.
The science does not need to apologize for this.
Heason and Hollister were not guessing. They were doing what scientists do with photographic evidence.
Applying the knowledge of the discipline to what the image shows. The case is closed.

The 1964 photograph was taken from a single angle. In black and white. With the limited

The living specimens in modern photographs are typically larger than the Eltonan object.
Different developmental stages may produce different morphologies. The specific conditions

One page. Proposing a return expedition to the Eltonan antenna coordinates. The note described

The note contains one observation about the photograph itself. Review of the original

In situ verification would resolve this discrepancy. The proposal was not funded.
The conference note was not published. It sits in a file at the institution.
A single page among hundreds of unfunded proposals from that year.
Noting that the identification is accepted. That the visual evidence does not entirely

And then the case was closed. And the ship went on. And the ship made a discovery
that was larger than any unexplained photograph. And the photograph became a footnote.
This is the Eltonan's real legacy. This is what the ship is remembered for.
Not frame 1032. 1965.
One year after the antenna photograph. The Eltonan is on its 19th Antarctic voyage.
The chief scientist aboard is a graduate student named Walter Pittman.
Pittman has been assigned to collect magnetic measurements across the Pacific Antarctic ridge.
A mid ocean ridge system running through the southeastern Pacific. The boundary between the
Pacific plate and the Antarctic plate. One of the most geologically active regions on the ocean floor.
He uses a magnetometer towed behind the ship. The instrument measures the magnetic intensity
of the ocean crust beneath the survey track. As the ship crosses the ridge, the magnetometer reads
the magnetic signature of the rock on either side. What Pittman records is a profile. A profile that
shows on either side of the Pacific Antarctic ridge. A pattern of magnetic reversals.
Alternating bands of rock magnetized in opposite directions. The record of the earth's magnetic
field flipping polarity repeatedly over millions of years as new crust formed at the ridge and
spread outward. This pattern is not new knowledge. The theory of sea floor spreading, first proposed
by Harry Hess in 1960, predicted that such a pattern should exist. What Pittman's profile
shows is the pattern with near perfect symmetry. The bands on the west side of the ridge mirror
the bands on the east side with the precision that removes all ambiguity. The sea floor is not
just spreading. The sea floor is spreading symmetrically. New crust forming at the ridge
and moving outward in both directions at the same rate. Recording the magnetic reversals of the
earth's field in a symmetrical tape recorder written in rock. The El Tianan 19 profile.
That is what it is called. Other researchers working in the same period had found similar
patterns in other ocean basins. But the El Tianan 19 profile was the clearest. The most symmetrical.
The most unambiguous. Pittman presented the data at the American Geophysical Union in April of 1966.
The audience understood what they were seeing. He published in Science in December of 1966.
The El Tianan 19 profile is called the magic profile. It is called the smoking gum of plate

That the ocean floor is being continuously created at mid ocean ridges
and consumed at the deep trenches where old crusts subdux back into the mantle.
The earth is not static. The surface of the planet is alive. Moving. Creating. Destroying.
Rearranging itself over millions of years in a geological cycle that makes the continents and

It finds what is there to be found. The El Tianan conducted 52 Antarctic research cruises
